items.decisionBoundary: Classify caller-owned input, temporary allocations, and the separately returned result according to the declared space convention.

Without identifying the required output first, the same structure may be misclassified as either result storage or working memory. Separate reporting avoids double-counting.
Space accounting begins with the contract, then separates input, result, and temporary state.

items.decisionBoundary: Advance the read boundary for every consumed input occurrence, but advance write only when an occurrence is retained.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Suppose [2, 3, 4] is filtered to keep even values. After retaining 2, read = 1 and write = 1 at the next loop boundary. The current value 3 is read and rejected, so no assignment occurs and write stays 1. Advancing read to 2 records that 3 was consumed; the valid prefix [0, 1) still contains exactly [2].
A rejected value consumes input but produces no output position.

items.decisionBoundary: Construct grouped output by expanding each positive per-value count while preserving the specified value order.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “A frequency count for each distinct value.”. A set can tell whether a value appeared, but it cannot distinguish one occurrence from five. A frequency count retains the exact multiplicity needed to reproduce grouped output.
Preserving multiplicity requires retaining the number of occurrences, not merely presence.
blocks.title: Decision rule

blocks.text: Why the other choices fail

items: A set containing each value once. — Presence state collapses all positive counts into one fact and loses multiplicity.
A single variable holding the first value. — A single value cannot describe the counts of the remaining distinct values.
One boolean indicating whether any duplicate exists. — Knowing that some duplicate exists does not identify which values repeat or how often.

messages.text: Knowing that some duplicate exists does not identify which values repeat or how often.

items.decisionBoundary: Report work for every input, count returned storage as output, and count only other algorithm-allocated working memory as auxiliary space.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “It can be O(n) time and O(k) auxiliary space, where k is the number of distinct values.”. The scan performs O(n) expected work under the standard hash-set model. The set may contain one entry for every distinct input value, so its auxiliary space is O(k), which is O(n) in the worst case.
One pass constrains the number of iterations, not the amount of retained state.
blocks.title: Decision rule

blocks.text: Why the other choices fail

items: It is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space because it uses only one loop. — A single loop does not imply constant space; the set grows with the number of distinct values.
It is necessarily O(n²) because the set grows during the scan. — Growing state does not by itself make the running time quadratic.
It is O(1) total time because set membership is expected O(1). — Expected O(1) membership applies per operation, not to the entire scan of n elements.

messages.text: Expected O(1) membership applies per operation, not to the entire scan of n elements.

Growing state does not by itself make the running time quadratic.

items.decisionBoundary: Compare each character count when order is irrelevant but exact multiplicity matters.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “Build character-frequency arrays and compare all counters.” Because order is irrelevant, positions need not be preserved. However, presence alone is insufficient: “aab” and “abb” have the same distinct characters and the same length but different counts. Comparing all 26 counters preserves and checks exactly the required multiplicities.
Equal multiplicities require count state for every relevant character.
blocks.title: Decision rule

blocks.text: Why the other choices fail

items: Compare only the sets of characters that appear. — Sets cannot distinguish different multiplicities of the same characters.
Compare only the first character of each string. — The first position does not summarize the remaining characters or their counts.
Equal lengths alone prove equal multiplicities. — Equal total length does not imply that each character count matches.

messages.text: The first position does not summarize the remaining characters or their counts.

Sets cannot distinguish different multiplicities of the same characters.

items.decisionBoundary: Track both the membership and stable ordering of retained values in the processed input prefix.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “At every loop boundary, write <= read.” The processed prefix is [0, read), and it can contribute at most read retained values, so write cannot be larger. During the next iteration, writing at an index below read changes only processed storage; writing at read is a self-write of the current source value.
The output boundary can lag behind the read position but must never move ahead of it.
blocks.title: Decision rule

blocks.text: Why the other choices fail

items: At every loop boundary, read <= write. — This permits write to exceed the processed-input count and move into unread territory.
At every loop boundary, write equals n. — Write should reflect retained count, which can be much smaller than n.
At every loop boundary, read equals write + 1. — Read and write are equal whenever every processed value has been retained.

messages.text: Read and write may be equal for long stretches when all values are retained.

Write should reflect retained count, which can be much smaller than n.

scoringEvidence.method: Tests call scoreQuestion and validateQuestion exported by scripts/content/question-contract.mjs, the repository canonical scorer and validator; they do not approximate adjacency scoring. Concrete input/output and complexity examples are checked as modeled examples. No app-consumer, admission, lock, or publication check is claimed.

oldOrderingAlternatives.whyAlternativeIsValid: Boundary cases can be designed after the equivalence contract is stated and before normalizer/comparison implementation; the current element does not say tests are executed only after implementation.
After the result contract is known, caller-owned input and temporary working allocations can be classified independently; the order of those two classifications does not change the bounds.
Leaving write unchanged is a no-op. Once rejection is known, consuming the source by advancing read and recording that write remains unchanged commute and yield the same next state.

scoringEvidence.newChoiceScoring: The seven replacements are validated with the canonical scorer: the keyed option receives 1/1 and each foil receives 0/1.
